sentences.text: The name Hypacrosaurus translates to "near the highest lizard," reflecting its status as a massive herbivore that rivaled the size of Tyrannosaurus while remaining slightly smaller.
This duck-billed dinosaur possessed a tall, hollow, rounded crest that was less upright and wide than that of Corythosaurus, featuring a small bony point at the rear.
Its back appeared exceptionally tall in profile due to neural spines projecting from the vertebrae that reached five to seven times the height of the vertebral bodies.
For decades an obscure genus, Hypacrosaurus remained unknown until 1987 when nests, eggs, and hatchlings were discovered in the Bear Paw Formation.
The species H. stebingeri produced rough, spherical eggs measuring 20 by 18.5 centimeters that contained embryos reaching 60 centimeters in length.
Scientists interpret a large, single-species group found in Montana as a herd that perished together following a volcanic ash fall.
The genus was formally named and described by Brown in 1913.
The type remains, which serve as the basis for the species description, were gathered in 1910 by Barnum Brown for the American Museum of Natural History.
Like other hadrosaurs, this animal was a herbivore capable of moving on two legs or four legs depending on the situation.
It utilized a grinding motion similar to chewing, relying on dental batteries packed with hundreds of teeth where only a few were functional at any given moment.
Feeding began with a broad beak that cropped vegetation, which the animal then held with a cheek-like organ to process plants ranging from the ground up to four meters high.
The hollow crest likely functioned as a resonance chamber for sound production and provided a visual signal for identifying sex or species.
Oxygen-isotope ratios indicate the dinosaur was a homeotherm and likely endothermic, though this conclusion conflicts with earlier studies based on nasal turbinates.
Research suggests the species reached reproductive maturity between two and three years of age, growing faster than its tyrannosaur predators like Albertosaurus and Tyrannosaurus.
Newly hatched individuals were approximately 1.7 meters long.
Evidence of a tyrannosaurid bite on the fibula suggests the animal was either prey or consumed as carrion by large theropods during the Late Cretaceous.
It is classified as a lambeosaurine hadrosaurid, a distinction recognized primarily from the unique features of its skull.
The genus belongs to the subfamily Corythosaurini.
Remains date from 75.0 to 69.5 million years ago, though other estimates place the range between 75 and 67 million years ago, found in Alberta, Canada, and Montana, United States.
Researchers debate whether the crest and nasal passages indicate endothermy, with some arguing the absence of nasal turbinates suggests the animal was not warm-blooded.

It is also debated whether Hypacrosaurus is paraphyletic; while Suzuki et al. proposed a strong link between Nipponosaurus and H. stebingeri in 2004, Evans and Reisz rejected this in 2007, finding them separate from Nipponosaurus but related to Corythosaurus and Olorotitan.
